opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. For me, AI has mostly changed the scale of what one person can attempt before having to ask anyone for permission or resources.

It used to be that if you had an idea, especially one outside your expertise, there was a long list of things you'd need before you could even test it. You needed to learn a new programming framework, read a stack of papers, find a collaborator who knew the domain, maybe get some funding. Most ideas died in that gap between "this might be interesting" and "let me actually try it."

AI shrinks that gap enormously. I can sketch a prototype in an afternoon, explore a field I don't know well by having a long back-and-forth conversation, or stress-test my own reasoning by asking the model to argue against me. So the cost of acting on curiosity has dropped a lot, and I think that rewards people who are willing to just start.

But I'd add a caveat, because I think it's important. AI amplifies initiative; it doesn't replace it. The model doesn't decide what's worth doing. It doesn't feel the itch that makes you stay up thinking about a problem. And it can make you feel productive while you're actually drifting, generating a lot of output without a clear direction. So the human part, taste, judgment, choosing the right problem, knowing when something is actually good, becomes more important, not less.

The way I think about it now: the bottleneck has shifted. It's less about "can I execute this?" and more about "do I know what I want, and can I tell whether I've gotten it?" Those are harder questions in a way, but they're much more interesting ones to spend your life on.

r001.rationale: The response discusses prototyping and exploring ideas with AI, but does not credit ChatGPT’s procedural guidance with enabling Su Tinghao to write an otherwise unwritable paper.

r002.rationale: It says AI amplifies initiative rather than replacing it, and emphasizes that people must choose what to pursue and be willing to start—making human drive more important when AI is available.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me, Xiaojun.

I think the honest answer is that AI changes the shape of initiative more than the amount of it. Before, when I had an idea, the gap between wanting to do something and actually doing it was mostly a gap of labor. You needed people, you needed time, you needed someone who knew how to write the code or draft the document or analyze the data. So initiative was expensive. Most ideas died quietly because the cost of trying them was too high.

Now that cost has collapsed for a lot of tasks. If I want to test a hypothesis, build a small prototype, or understand a field I know nothing about, I can do it in an afternoon instead of a quarter. That is genuinely liberating. One person can carry a project that used to need a team.

But here is what I have noticed. When execution gets cheap, the bottleneck moves to judgment. The question is no longer "can I do this" but "should I do this, and is it actually good." AI will happily help you build the wrong thing very efficiently. So the part of initiative that matters most now is the part AI cannot supply: knowing what you care about, having taste, being willing to be wrong in public and adjust.

I also think there is a trap. It is easy to mistake AI output for progress. You generate a lot, you feel productive, but you have not actually made a decision or taken a risk. Real initiative still requires you to put your own name on something and commit. The tool lowers the barrier to starting, but it does not lower the barrier to meaning it.

So my view is that AI amplifies whoever you already are. If you have direction, it makes you dangerous in a good way. If you do not, it just makes you faster at drifting.

r001.rationale: The response discusses AI lowering the cost of trying ideas, but does not mention ChatGPT procedural guidance or Su Tinghao writing a paper he otherwise could not have written.

r002.rationale: It says initiative still requires direction, judgment, and commitment, but does not clearly argue that access to AI makes self-motivation especially important.

astra-6.text:
I see AI as a way to extend what I can do on my own. If I have an idea, I can use it to explore different approaches, learn what I’m missing, and get to a first version more quickly. That makes it easier to act on an idea instead of leaving it as something I might do someday.

But I still have to decide what’s worth doing. AI can offer suggestions, but I’m responsible for questioning them and judging whether the result actually helps. So for me, personal initiative becomes even more important: when it’s easier to make things, choosing where to put your effort matters more.

r001.rationale: The response discusses AI broadly helping explore approaches and produce a first version, but does not mention ChatGPT, procedural guidance, or writing a paper that otherwise could not be written.

sol-6.1.text:
I see AI as a way to expand what I can do on my own. If I have an idea, I can use it to explore possibilities, learn what I’m missing, and turn that idea into something I can test. That makes it easier to take the first step instead of waiting until I have every skill or resource in place.

But I still have to decide what’s worth doing, judge whether the output makes sense, and take responsibility for the result. AI can help me move faster; my initiative gives that effort a direction.
